title: My Pill Tastes Sweet Today
youtube_title: Five months pregnant, she bit her pill. Why was it sweet?
logline: Five months pregnant, Nora Quinn only wants to carry her baby safely to term. But the pill her husband left out this morning tastes sweet, and by night the phone by her bed is gone.
hook: A silent dream: one pane of the Glass House cracks from corner to corner. A crooked glass bird drops past it, and a hand reaches into frame and catches it. She wakes to warm water and one pill. She bites down and frowns: “My pill tastes sweet today.”
mid_hook: Afternoon. The doorbell. Cole, Grant's driver, stands there in white gloves: “Mr. Whitlock sent me.” “Your phone's going in for repair.” She hands it over. The door shuts, and the glass house goes quiet except for the waves.
extra_hooks: Peg stands in the nursery doorway, staring at the floor-to-ceiling window: “Window that big.” “The whole bay can see in.” She picks the half-knitted hat up off the couch: “Stitches are loose.” “It'll come out too big.”
conflict: She wants to do what Dr. Brandt told her: rest, take her pills, get through the days. But the pill tastes wrong. She calls Grant and he laughs it off, “They changed the coating, babe,” then says her phone keeps dropping calls and he'll send his driver to take it in. Peg makes her weekly visit to find fault: the soup's bland, the nursery window's too big.
turn: Peg leaves after a whole day of nitpicking, and she calls back from the door: “Soup's in the fridge.” “Salt it yourself.” On TV, an ad: Grant cradles the Forever vase she blew at twenty-five, and his own voice says, “Whitlock Home. Made to last forever.” Her name is nowhere. She looks at the half pill again and murmurs: “The letters look wrong.”

cliffhanger.text: Past midnight, a cramp jolts her awake. She reaches for the nightstand. Empty. The phone never came back. She edges along the cold glass wall, one hand flat on the pane, and only one reflection moves with her.
cliffhanger.question: No phone. Who does she call?

spectacle: In the dream a single floor-to-ceiling pane cracks silently from corner to corner; a crooked glass bird drops past the crack and a hand catches it cleanly.
glamour_shot: Morning light through the floor-to-ceiling glass: Nora in a cream knit sweater, long hair loose, holds the half pill up to the window and squints at it, her profile as still as glass.
general_payoffs: She wraps the spat-out half pill in a tissue and tucks it in her coat pocket instead of throwing it away

title: The Light at the End of the Hall
youtube_title: No phone, no husband. A stranger stopped and made the call
logline: She drags herself to the front door for help, and a stranger whose face she never sees calls an ambulance. In the seventh-floor hallway at Merrow General, the one who comes isn't her husband. It's a doctor saying “I'm so sorry.”
hook: She pulls on her coat, the half-knitted hat still in her fist, and inches along the glass wall to the front door. Rain hits her face. She grabs the lamppost by the door, doubled over; its light flickers. Her clothes stay clean; only her face shows the pain.
mid_hook: A car brakes hard on the drive, headlights cutting through the rain. We see only a hand in a dark glove dialing 911: “Glass House, on the bluff.” “Pregnant woman.” “Hurry.” In the ambulance, close on her face, the same low voice: “Stay awake. Stay with me.”
extra_hooks: Merrow General, the seventh-floor hallway with no windows. At the far end a light flickers. On the bench beneath it, a soaked figure sits down, face in shadow, then stands, then sits again.
conflict: She has to hold on until someone comes. But her phone is gone, she's alone in the house, and her husband can't be reached all night.
turn: The one who saves her isn't her husband. It's someone whose face she never sees. All she will remember is a voice in her ear, over and over: “Stay awake.”

cliffhanger.text: Dr. Brandt crouches by her bed: “I'm so sorry.” Nora laughs once and shakes her head: “No. No, he's fine.” Then it breaks. She clutches the hat and screams: “Where's my baby?!” Nurse Kim holds her; Nora shoves her off: “Don't touch me! Call Grant!” At the end of the hall, the light flickers.
cliffhanger.question: Where was her husband?

spectacle: A rainy night on the drive: the lamppost at the Glass House door flickering, headlights breaking through the rain to stop at her feet; Merrow General's seventh floor, a long windowless hallway, the light at its end going bright, dark, bright.
glamour_shot: Rain runs down her long hair as she holds the lamppost and looks up; the headlights wash her pale profile cold blue.
general_payoffs: A stranger calls the ambulance for her and keeps her talking all the way
The hat stays in her fist the whole way; even screaming, she won't let it go

title: We're Still Young
youtube_title: She waited alone till dawn. He said: “We're still young.”
logline: Nora needs to know where her husband was that night. He arrives at dawn, says he was at his mom's and his phone died, and gets a glass of water in the face. But his phone keeps lighting up.
hook: Dawn. The elevator opens. Grant's umbrella is still dripping, his rimless glasses fogged. He takes her hand, his voice warm as a keynote: “We're still young.”
mid_hook: Nurse Kim, changing the IV: “The man who called 911?” “Not your husband.” Nora rips her hand from Grant's, grabs the water glass off the nightstand and throws it in his face: “Where were you?!” “I was on the floor! Alone!” The whole nurses' station turns to look.
extra_hooks: He says: “I was at Mom's.” “My phone died.” The words are barely out when the phone in his jacket buzzes. Then again.
conflict: She needs to know where her husband was and why she couldn't reach him. All he gives her is “I was at Mom's” and “My phone died.”
turn: She thought he was just late. Then the nurse says “Not your husband,” and the phone that's supposedly dead won't stop buzzing. Dripping, Grant wipes his glasses and keeps his voice low: “Nor. People can hear.” For the first time, she knows he's lying, and so does the hallway.

cliffhanger.text: He steps out to dry off. On the nightstand his phone lights up; a text (text added in post): “Got the curtain measurements. —S.” She stares at that S. He comes back and, without a word, flips the phone face down.

glamour_shot: Dawn light slices through the blinds onto her pale profile, wet glass still in her hand; she watches that phone, and for the first time her eyes go cold.

title: The Old One Couldn't Be Fixed
youtube_title: Her new phone had no numbers in it. Not even her doctor's
logline: Nora wants to tell Grant about the sweet pill, but he hands her a new phone first. He holds the account, he has talked to the floor, and every line she had to the outside world now runs through him.
hook: He pockets the face-down phone and pulls a new box from a paper bag: “The old one couldn't be fixed.” “Got you a new one.” She turns it on. The contacts screen is blank.
mid_hook: She says: “That pill.” “It was sweet.” He smiles and tucks the blanket around her: “You're exhausted.” She hits the call button and asks for Dr. Brandt. The on-call doctor: “She's off till Monday.” He glances at Grant: “Your husband mentioned you're upset.”
conflict: She wants someone to hear “The pill was sweet.” With one “You're exhausted” Grant takes the words away. He has already told the seventh floor, “My wife's confused. Route everything through me,” and he swaps out her phone, her number and every person she could call.
turn: She thinks the new phone is thoughtful. Then her old number is disconnected, and when she tries to sign into her account, it rejects her password with a flat buzz. Grant, mildly: “I'm the account holder, babe. I changed it for you.” Dr. Brandt, her friends, her old studio, all gone. Her only line to the world runs through him.

cliffhanger.text: He gets up, lifts her coat off the chair, and slides a hand into the pocket: “I'll take this home and wash it.” “Bring you a clean one tomorrow.” His fingers stop on the wad of tissue.
cliffhanger.question: Will he find the half pill?

title: The Wall at the End of the Hall
youtube_title: Mother-in-law packed for a month. Then she saw the wall
logline: Nora has to keep the half pill in her pocket. Her mother-in-law arrives with a suitcase, sobs alone at the wall at the end of the hall, then walks in sharp-tongued, and backs her son's story.
hook: She clamps a hand over the coat: “I'm cold.” Grant pauses, then smiles and lets go, draping the coat back over her shoulders: “Okay.” “No washing.” Her hand slides into the pocket and closes tight around the tissue.
mid_hook: Peg steps off the elevator with a big suitcase and a thermos. She walks right past the room, down to the flickering light at the end of the hall, and lays her palm on the blank wall. Then her forehead. Her shoulders shake; she sobs out loud. Ten seconds. She blows her nose and turns around.
extra_hooks: Peg comes in dry-eyed and plants the thermos on the table: “Drink.” “It's bland.” Nora looks past her at Grant: “He was with you last night?” Peg looks at her son. One beat too long. “...Sure.”
conflict: Before discharge she has to protect the half pill and face her mother-in-law. Grant tells Peg, “You'll stay at my place, Mom.” Peg: “I packed for her house. Take me there.” He gives in, “After one stop,” and books Nora a car home alone. Peg: “You're putting her in a cab?” “I've got a meeting.” “Some husband.”
turn: She thought Peg came to gloat. Instead Peg packed a month of clothes to cook for her, and lied for her son with a face gone grey. Then, in her son's car, something drains the rest of the color from it.

cliffhanger.text: In the back of Grant's car, Cole driving, Peg feels in the center console for a tissue and touches a folded receipt. One glance and she freezes. Grant, beside her, looks up from his phone: “Mom?” “What's wrong?” She folds it small and tucks it into her ledger: “Nothing.”

title: They Changed the Locks
youtube_title: Her key won't turn. His lawyer says she signed it all away
logline: Home from the hospital, Nora's key won't turn. Her husband's lawyer is waiting inside with a property agreement she never signed, the woman from the text is hanging curtains, and the deputy she calls shrugs.
hook: The car stops at the top of the drive. She climbs out holding the hospital bag and puts her key in the Glass House lock. It won't turn. She tries again. The lock is new, so shiny it hurts.
mid_hook: The door opens from inside. A man with slicked-back hair and gold-rimmed glasses, fountain pen in hand: “Mrs. Whitlock.” “Leonard Fisk, Grant's attorney.” “Two documents.” “One for you to sign.” “One you already signed.” She steps past him: “Excuse me. I live here.”
extra_hooks: In the living room, installers are hanging heavy grey curtains over the floor-to-ceiling glass. A woman with short hair and red lipstick directs them in heels: “Left side, a little more.” “This house is too see-through.”
conflict: She wants into her own home. Fisk has divorce papers waiting for her signature and a separate property agreement: “Under the agreement, it's all Grant's separate property.” She calls the police. A county deputy reads the papers on the steps, in front of Fisk, Sienna and the installers: “It's a civil matter, ma'am.” “Take it to court.”

title: Ten Minutes

logline: Nora has ten minutes to take what's hers. No jewelry, no money. She loses the nursery to a curtain rod and walks out with her sketches from before the marriage and her mother's glass, the Keepsake block.

title: Half a Pill
youtube_title: First night out, she broke down. Then Peg told the truth
logline: Her first night out of the house, Nora finally breaks down over the baby, and Peg holds her. Then Nora takes out the half pill she's hidden all day, and in the dark Peg takes back her lie.
hook: Peg takes the half-knitted hat from the hospital bag, looks at the loose stitches, and says as she writes in her ledger: “Hat. Mine.” She tucks it into her knitting bag. Nora breaks: “He was a boy, Peg.” “I was going to name him.” She can't get another word out.
mid_hook: Nora unfolds the tissue from her coat pocket: the bitten half pill. She sniffs it, touches a fingertip to it, then to her tongue. Sweet. Peg grabs her wrist: “Don't.” She pulls a zip-top bag from her knitting bag: “Put it in this.”
extra_hooks: Through the gap in the curtains: a black car across the street, lights off, a figure in the driver's seat, not moving.
conflict: All she has is half a sweet pill, a grief she hasn't let out, and nobody who believes her. The one person who might know the truth, Peg, keeps her mouth shut tighter than her ledger.
turn: Peg sits on Nora's bed and holds her for the first time, both of them crying, Peg hoarse: “I know, honey.” “I know.” Then, looking at the bag: “We see the doctor tomorrow.” A woman who has taken her son's side all her life is telling Nora to look into him.

cliffhanger.text: Nora: “Peg, what do you know?” Peg reaches over and switches off the lamp. A long silence in the dark. Then: “He wasn't at my place.” “That night.” “He wasn't with me.” The red neon outside blinks on and off across Peg's open eyes.
